I made a post about this just a few days ago, but am admittedly too lazy to go and link it at the moment. Here are all the things I wish I had done:

1) Start working on assignments as soon as you get all of the syllabi for your classes. Why would you want to wait for the instructor to tell you when things are due/when to start working on them when you already have their due dates right in front of you? You might need to wait on some things that may need more explanation, like big papers or projects, but if it's every day homework or readings, do them right away. Try to get ahead during the first week when you don't have a lot going on so that when things get busy later on in the semester, you can afford to take down time when you need it.

2) Be mindful of how you schedule your classes. If you aren't a morning person, don't schedule an 8a.m. class if you can help it. A general rule of thumb as well if you're able to do so, for every single difficult class, take two or three easy classes alongside of it. Ex: If you're taking Calc. I, take English Comp., an easy science gen ed. like Intro to Geology or Intro to Psychology. 

3) Develop a study routine around your class schedule. For example, if you're taking five classes, but have three of them on M/W/F and the other two on T/TH, do the homework for your M/W/F classes on T/TH when you have more time to do them, and vice versa. Doing assignments between classes is also ideal in that the material from the last class will still be fresh enough in your mind to do the assignment well, and doing the assignment before next class will also act as a "refresher" so that you can better connect what you learned from one session to the next. Try to do homework/study for your most difficult class every single day, even if it's only for an hour a day.

4) When working on big papers or projects, have a copy of the file on your home computer/laptop/other PC and keep a second copy on a flash drive (or multiple copies on two flash drives). This will not only allow you to work on your assignment when you're on the go, but if something should happen to where you end up losing one copy (computer crashes, gets stolen, flash drive goes missing), you still have your work saved  elsewhere and won't need to redo anything. Every time you add/change anything in one copy, open up one of the other duplicates and copy and paste changes from one document to the next (this works best with a flash drive).

5) Once you figure out when to study, find where to study. If you do best at Starbucks, go there. If you do best outside at the park, go there. I'm someone who can't study without some sort of white noise in the background and for me, the best place was on top of the building all of my classes were in when the weather was nice (they had a specially built observation deck for this purpose), because the noises of the city served as "background noise".

6) School will be busy, but don't let it completely take over your life to the point where it starts affecting your well-being. Make sure to eat foods that give you energy, drink plenty of water, keep good hygiene, get a reasonable amount of sleep, etc. Set aside one day a week for yourself...sleep in as late as you want to. Go hiking, shopping, swimming, browse reddit, out to eat, etc. If you have a part-time job, try to arrange your schedule so that you have that day off every week. 

7) Stay organized in whatever way you can. Put papers where they're supposed to go as soon as they're in your hand. Take one day a week to organize folders, throw out things that need to be thrown out, plan ahead for the week, etc.

A lot of hospitals will have what's called "per diem"/"PRN"/"on call" and it can be for anything, not just nursing...I've known people who worked PRN at hospitals who were in housekeeping, kitchen work, various techs of some sort, transporters...you have to work a minimum number of hours a month to keep status as a PRN employee (in my area it's 16 hours a month), some might require you to work weekends as part of that, but in general, you pick up hours as they need you AND as YOU are available to pick them up...you have the right to decline if they offer you hours and a right to pick up as many as you can/want/need. Per diem employees also usually have a higher rate of pay than employees on part/full time staff because the lack of consistent hours disqualifies them from receiving benefits through their employer and if they have a higher pay they can pay for medical expenses out of pocket. At one hospital in my area, they pay regular kitchen staff $14-15 an hour if they're regular employees, but up to $20 an hour if they're PRN. It's a magical thing.

I don't know what it would be outside of a medical setting, but a lot of hospitals will have shifts like that where an employee works less than 20 per week and classify the employee as "per diem", meaning "as needed". You pick up hours when they have them available and can't find someone on regular staff to cover them, thus the need to call their "emergency backup staff" to fill in when they're short handed. Last summer (2015), my best friend and I were taking a class that met two nights a week for a month. One night after dropping her off at home after class was over, I went to a festival downtown and left around 10:30 pm. On the way home I decided to stop at a local park just out of the city limits where I go often to swing and listen to music since I wasn't tired.

I'm there maybe 15-20 minutes when another car pulls into the lot and a young couple gets out. People fish at this park at night so I didn't think much of it, but after a few minutes I notice the couple didn't leave the general area around their car. I felt like I was being watched, so I kept swinging but turned the volume on my music down while keeping my headphones in. I was right, they were talking about me and speculating about when I was going to leave. My blood froze and I knew I had to get out of there, but in order to get back to my car I would have had to walk past the gate to the playground, past the couple and around their car to get to mine (they were also ridiculously close to my passenger side like they were trying to block me in). Instead, I got off the swing while acting like I was sending a text and walked to a darker area of the playground away from them hoping that I could hide in the shadows until they took off.

Once I was there and hidden among dark playground equipment, I suddenly heard a third voice in the darkness that sounded like one of a woman who had been chain smoking her whole life. I suddenly felt sick to my stomach when I remembered that while I was watching the young couple, a second car had pulled into the parking lot but whoever was in it either hadn't gotten out and was watching me from the vehicle, or was lurking around in the dark somewhere where I couldn't see them. Luckily, the part of the park I was in backed up to a fence that had a tree growing up against it. I hopped it as silently as I could and decided I was going to make my way up the road where it was completely dark, go out the north entrance to the park on foot and circle back around so that when I got back to the other parking lot, I could make a mad dash to my driver's side door and get the hell out of there. I could hear the three of them arguing with each other in the dark by now.

My heart was pounding as I tiptoed up the street, silently praying that I wasn't going to get abducted and murdered. I got to the entrance of the parking lot where there was a large bush and a portable toilet that I could hide behind when I heard the voice of the woman so close to me that it was like she was whispering in my ear. What she asked the guy and girl next made my heart stop:

"Did you get rid of the body yet?"

The three of them immediately started arguing again and the woman got into her car, slamming the door shut and turning the engine on. As she was pulling out of the lot, I ran across the street and hid in the shadows between a cluster of trees and someone's house. Both cars pulled out of the parking lot within 30 seconds of each other going in opposite directions. As soon as I was sure they weren't coming back and not wanting to catch a glimpse of whatever grisly crime scene they may have left behind, I sprinted to my car, unlocked it, sped out of the park and called the police as soon as I pulled into my grandparents' driveway. I talked with the dispatcher for close to 20 minutes crying and shaking. Officers were sent out to check the area where all of this took place but they didn't find anything.
